title: 'Mega Masters' Hearings Pack Immigration Courts With 100-Plus Cases as Deportation Strategy Expands
excerpt: Immigration attorneys say the new tactic of scheduling mass hearings targets people without lawyers and is designed to generate deportation orders at scale.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • US immigration courts are now holding 'mega masters' hearings with over 100 cases at once.
  • These hearings disproportionately affect individuals without legal representation, increasing deportation orders.
  • Cases originally scheduled for 2027-2029 are being rescheduled with little notice, risking automatic removal.
  • The DOJ hired 153 new immigration judges this year while firing those with immigrant representation backgrounds.

  • US immigration courts are scheduling 'mega masters' hearings with 100 or more people at a time, up from the typical two to three dozen
  • Immigration attorneys and AILA say the hearings disproportionately target people without legal representation and are designed to generate deportation orders at scale
  • People whose original hearings were set for 2027-2029 are being pulled forward with little or no notice, meaning those who miss the rescheduled date receive automatic removal orders
  • The DOJ has hired 153 new immigration judges this fiscal year while simultaneously firing judges with backgrounds in immigrant representation

US immigration courts have adopted a new and unprecedented tactic to accelerate deportations: scheduling mass hearings with more than 100 people at a time, a strategy that immigration attorneys say is designed to generate removal orders at scale while sidelining due process protections.

The practice, dubbed "mega masters" by the immigration bar, has been documented in courts in Chicago, Boston, Chelmsford, Massachusetts, Baltimore, and the Annandale, Virginia court, according to attorneys and the American Immigration Lawyers Association. Dallas is expected to adopt the format next.

"Normally, these master calendars will have 10 people, maybe sometimes 15, but usually in that range. The judge opened the hearing and said well, we have 100 cases on today's docket," said Joseph M. Perez, a Virginia-based immigration attorney with more than two decades of experience, in an account shared with ABC News.

How the Strategy Works

Master calendar hearings are an immigrant's first appearance before a judge — the stage where they learn their rights, hear the charges against them, and begin building a case to stay in the US. Traditionally held in groups of two to three dozen, these initial hearings are now being packed with 100 or more respondents.

The critical mechanism is rescheduling. Cases originally set for 2027, 2028, or 2029 are being pulled forward to imminent dates, often with little or no advance notice sent by mail or electronically. If a person does not appear — whether because they never received the notice or arrived late to an overcrowded courthouse — the judge issues an in absentia removal order that authorises immediate deportation.

"They're anticipating that the majority will not show up and they'll just be able to say that they completed X number of cases because they'll be in absentia orders of removal."

— Texas-based immigration attorney, speaking to NPR on condition of anonymity

Due Process Concerns

"The major concern is that this is going to be a group of people without attorneys, that they're not going to have gotten proper notice," said Vanessa Dojaquez-Torres, practising policy counsel at AILA. "So it's almost like they are being designed to increase how many people get deportation orders automatically."

In Baltimore, one judge's morning docket sheet listed 120 names — roughly triple the number from the week before. Marcia Bravo, one of those listed, told reporters she was "really scared to come" after receiving a hearing notice just two weeks earlier, but knew the alternative was an automatic deportation order.

Attorney Briana Carlson described a case in which her client's hearing was advanced from July to an earlier date without any notice to the legal team. Her paralegal only discovered the change by checking an online portal.

Courts Lose and Gain Judges Simultaneously

The push for speed comes alongside a massive restructuring of the immigration judiciary. The DOJ has hired 153 immigration judges this fiscal year — the most in any year — including 77 sworn in last week alongside five temporary military lawyers. Yet the agency also lost more than 100 judges last year through firings, with an NPR analysis finding that judges who had previously represented immigrant clients were disproportionately targeted.

For the Indian community, the implications are significant. Indians in deportation proceedings, adjustment-of-status limbo, or navigating asylum claims face the same compressed timelines and notice failures as other immigrants. The combination of mass hearings, minimal notice, and a judiciary reshaped to prioritise removal efficiency means that even those with strong legal claims risk losing them before they can be heard.
